# A certified failure of the affine critical-root / concave-floor moment bound

The proposed numerical statement was as follows. Let d>=2, let
I={0,...,N-1}, and let i be a source index. Suppose that a_j is strictly
positive and affine, with a_i=k>=d/(d+1), and

    sum_{j in I} (j-i) a_j^(d-1)=0.

Suppose v_j>=a_j is a positive concave sequence and v_i=1. Is it then true
that

    sum_j v_j^d <= (2/Gamma_d) sum_j a_j^d,
    Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d ?

The answer is NO. The following is an exact counterexample, using only ten
integer sites. It is a counterexample to this numerical lemma, not to (OC):
the hypotheses do not include a globally deepest point of an actual body.

## 1. Exact counterexample

Take d=6, I={0,...,9}, and i=8. Define the polynomial

    P(c)=35c^5+375c^4+2550c^3+8670c^2+9195c-11805.

It is strictly increasing for c>=0, since every coefficient of P' is
positive. Direct exact evaluations give

    P(2/3)=-239945/243<0,
    P(3/4)=1198965/1024>0.

Thus there is a unique positive real root c, and 2/3<c<3/4. Set

    a_j=(j+c)/(9+c),    v_j=1       (j=0,...,9).

Every a_j is strictly positive, the sequence is affine, and a_j<=1=v_j.
The whole-root sequence v is positive and concave. Its source value is one.
The source cap root satisfies

    k=a_8=(8+c)/(9+c)>6/7,

because 7(8+c)-6(9+c)=2+c>0.

Expansion of the finite power sum gives the polynomial identity

    sum_{j=0}^9 (j-8)(j+c)^5 = -P(c).

Since P(c)=0, division by (9+c)^5 proves the required critical balance
exactly:

    sum_{j=0}^9 (j-8)a_j^5=0.

Write B=sum_{j=0}^9 a_j^6. For j<9 the function
(c+j)/(c+9) is strictly increasing in c, as its derivative is
(9-j)/(c+9)^2>0; the j=9 term is constant. Hence B is strictly increasing in
c. At the rational upper bound c=3/4 its value is

    B(3/4)=2280098630/1172914587 < 39/20.

The displayed strict rational inequality is certified by

    39*1172914587-20*2280098630=141696293>0.

On the other hand,

    5 Gamma_6 = 5*(6/7)^6 > 39/20,

because

    100*6^6-39*7^6 = 77289>0.

Consequently

    B < 39/20 < 5 Gamma_6,

while sum_j v_j^6=10. Thus

    sum_j v_j^6 = 10 > (2/Gamma_6) B,

strictly contradicting the proposed bound. This proof uses exact integers,
rationals, monotonicity, and the intermediate value theorem only.

## 2. The valid reduction to two affine majorants

Although it does not save the failed bound, the following exact reduction
explains how to search the stated numerical problem without a numerical
convex optimization claim.

Assume the numerical hypotheses, with N>=2. The positive critical weights
force 0<i<N-1: if i is an endpoint, all terms (j-i)a_j^(d-1) have the same
sign and at least one is nonzero. Put R=N-1 and

    h_j=v_j-a_j>=0,    h_i=1-k.

Since a is affine and v is concave, h is concave. Choose a supporting affine
majorant L_j=(1-k)+s(j-i) to h at i; such a line exists for a concave finite
sequence by taking s between its right and left adjacent differences.
The monotonicity of consecutive differences proves L_j>=h_j at every j.
In particular its endpoint values are nonnegative, and therefore

    -(1-k)/(R-i) <= s <= (1-k)/i.

The convex function s -> sum_j [a_j+(1-k)+s(j-i)]^d is maximized over this
interval at an endpoint. All its bases are nonnegative on this interval.
Because v_j<=a_j+L_j and the d-th power is increasing on nonnegative roots,
one gets the sharp bound

    sum_j v_j^d <= max(sum_j (v_j^-)^d, sum_j (v_j^+)^d),

where the two affine sequences are

    v_j^- = a_j+(1-k)(R-j)/(R-i),
    v_j^+ = a_j+(1-k)j/i.

Both are themselves feasible: they are affine, lie above a, and have source
value one. Thus the maximum over all feasible concave whole-root sequences
is EXACTLY this two-point maximum. No vertex enumeration is needed.

For the counterexample in Section 1, the constant choice v_j=1 already
violates the target inequality, so maximizing over these two affine
majorants is unnecessary.

## 3. Polynomial growth reformulation and the missing bound

Normalize a_j=k[1+t_*(j-i)] and let

    Phi(t)=sum_j [1+t(j-i)]^d.

Its domain of strictly positive roots is
(-1/(R-i),1/i), and the critical balance is Phi'(t_*)=0.
Writing delta=(1-k)/k, each extremal affine whole-root profile divided by k
has the form

    [1+t_*(j-i)] + delta[1+e(j-i)],

with e an endpoint of the nonnegative-root slope interval. Since
k>=d/(d+1), one has 0<=delta<=1/d, and the expression is nondecreasing in
delta at every site. At delta=1/d it equals

    (1+1/d) [1+((d t_*+e)/(d+1))(j-i)].

Accordingly, the proposed moment lemma would follow from the polynomial
claim

    Phi((d t_*+e)/(d+1)) <= 2 Phi(t_*).

The exact counterexample above also disproves that claim in the relevant
class: the affine-majorant reduction and delta monotonicity would otherwise
imply the contradicted numerical bound. Stationarity and convexity alone
supply no such factor-two growth control.
